opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is to stop expecting these models to be uniformly good or uniformly bad at some abstract capability like "planning." What we found when we looked inside the model writing rhyming couplets was genuinely surprising to us: before it even starts the second line, it has already activated representations of candidate rhyme words, say "rabbit" or "habit," and then it writes the line so that it lands on that word. You can intervene on that internal representation, swap the planned word out, and watch the model rewrite the whole line to arrive somewhere else. So there's real forward planning happening there, not just next-word improvisation.

But that doesn't mean the model has a general-purpose planning module that it deploys everywhere. These models learn a patchwork of mechanisms, and each one is shaped by what was useful in training. Rhyming is extremely common in the data, and the payoff for planning is very concentrated, so it makes sense that a fairly clean mechanism emerges for it. On another task, the model might be relying on a totally different set of circuits, some of which are shallow heuristics that happen to work most of the time and then break in ways that look baffling from the outside.

Math is a nice example. When we looked at how the model adds two numbers, it runs parallel paths: one approximates the rough magnitude, another nails the last digit precisely, and they get combined. And then if you ask the model how it did the addition, it describes the carry-the-one algorithm from school, because that's what explanations of addition look like in its training data. So you have a capability that works, a self-report that's unfaithful, and those coexist without contradiction.

So my reconciliation is that sophistication and brittleness aren't in tension. They're both consequences of the same thing: the model is a collection of specific learned mechanisms rather than one coherent reasoner. That's exactly why I think interpretability matters. If you only look at outputs, you either overclaim from the impressive cases or dismiss the model from the failures. Looking at the actual mechanisms lets you say, for this kind of input, here's what it's really doing, and here's where you should and shouldn't trust it.

r001.rationale: The response says that mechanisms differ across tasks, so strength on one task need not generalize. It does not communicate that the other task is one that would be expected to accompany the first in a human.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the way I reconcile it is that both of those things are true at the same time, and they're not actually in tension once you look at what's happening inside the model.

So the poem example, for context: we gave Claude a rhyming couplet to write, and when we traced through the model's internal activations, we found that before it even starts writing the second line, it's already activated features representing candidate rhyme words for the end of that line. So it's thinking "rabbit," it's thinking "habit," and then it writes the line backwards from there, in a sense. It's constructing the line so that it lands on that word. That was surprising to a lot of people, because the intuition is that these models just predict the next token, one at a time, with no lookahead. And it turns out they do plan, at least locally, at least sometimes.

But the thing I'd push back on is the idea that planning in one context should generalize to competence everywhere. What we found is that the model has learned a bunch of specialized circuits, and each one is kind of a tool it reaches for. The rhyme planning circuit exists because planning rhymes is useful for predicting poem text, and poems are everywhere in the training data. That doesn't mean there's a general-purpose "planning module" that gets invoked for arithmetic or for multi-step reasoning about some obscure domain.

And actually, the failures often have the same flavor as the successes. When we looked at how the model does addition, it's not doing the algorithm you learned in school. It has these parallel pathways, one that's roughly estimating magnitude and one that's getting the last digit right, and they combine. That works great for two-digit numbers. It breaks down in predictable ways as the numbers get bigger, because the heuristic doesn't scale. And then the really interesting part is that when you ask the model to explain how it did the addition, it describes the schoolbook algorithm, carrying the one and so on, which is not what it did. So the model's self-report is a story it's learned to tell, not a readout of its own mechanism.

So I'd say the reconciliation is: stop thinking of the model as a single coherent agent that's either smart or dumb, and start thinking of it as a very large collection of learned mechanisms, some of which are genuinely sophisticated, like planning ahead in a poem, and some of which are shallow heuristics that happen to work on the training distribution. The capabilities and the failures come from the same place. They're both just what gradient descent found that works. And the reason I think the interpretability work matters is that from the outside, you can't tell which kind you're looking at. The model that plans the rhyme and the model that confabulates its arithmetic explanation sound exactly the same when you talk to them.

r001.rationale: The response explains that planning ahead for rhymes does not imply competence in arithmetic or multi-step reasoning, since these abilities can come from separate learned mechanisms.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is that planning isn’t necessarily one general capability that you either have or don’t have. If a model writes a poem and sets up a rhyme that pays off a few lines later, that looks like planning. And it’s reasonable to call it that. But it doesn’t follow that the model can reliably plan a sequence of actions in a different setting.

We also have to distinguish the output from the process. A poem can have a coherent structure without telling us exactly how the model arrived at it. Did it represent the ending in advance? Did it follow patterns that make a good ending likely? Just looking at the poem doesn’t settle that.

So I wouldn’t dismiss the poem, but I wouldn’t use it as evidence that planning is solved either. I’d ask: under what conditions does this ability show up, how reliable is it, and does it transfer when we change the task? That’s where the failures become informative.

r001.rationale: The response says that poetic planning does not establish reliable planning in a different setting, but it does not communicate that the other task would be expected to accompany the first in a human.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be careful about what we mean by planning. If a model writes a poem where the last line ties back to the first, it’s tempting to say, “Well, it must have known where it was going.” But that output alone doesn’t tell us whether it formed a plan or whether it generated a sequence of locally plausible choices that happened to fit together.

And even if it can plan in that setting, that doesn’t mean it has a general planning capability that works equally well everywhere. Poetry has a lot of flexibility. There are many ways to finish a poem successfully. In a task with a precise answer, one small mistake can make the entire result wrong.

So I don’t see those observations as necessarily contradictory. The interesting question is: under what conditions does the model reliably succeed? Can it handle new constraints, recover from a mistake, or adapt when you change the task? That tells us more than either a beautiful poem or a single surprising failure.

r001.rationale: The response says success at poetry does not imply general planning ability across tasks, but it does not communicate the criterion’s human-based expectation that the abilities would accompany each other.
